utterances.text: Raskovic opposed Milosevic in public. He criticised him on a number of occasions, on a couple of occasions. I know that he spoke of the impotence of the JNA at a meeting in Lapac. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you -- on this other occasion around this meeting in Geneva, what did Mr. Milosevic talk to you about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main topic of discussion always was the question of our security and what would happen to the Serbs in SAO Krajina, their destiny. That was always the main issue. And he always said, "The JNA would protect you," he said, and, "You have the right to remain in Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you meet Mr. Milosevic in March 1991 around this -- at a time when demonstrations took place in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before that, I had a conversation with him, at the beginning of March, in connection with the events in Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What was it about, the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an incident in Pakrac, a conflict between Serbs and the Croatian police, when the JNA also intervened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know about this event. You do not need to tell us the event as such, but what did you talk with Mr. Milosevic about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called him up by telephone to ask him what was going on in Pakrac, and he said, "Don't worry. Everything will be okay. You can go to Knin."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he informed on what was going on in Pakrac at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what he said, I understood that he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I was actually asking you about contacts with Mr. Milosevic at the time when demonstrations took place. Did you see him then? When did you see him, and what was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the demonstrations, I was called by Matkovic, a senior official in the SBS, to come to a counter-rally organised by the SBS against the opposition that was demonstrating. I avoided going. Then I was asked to send a letter, a message to the participants in the rally and to come to Belgrade after that, to be in Belgrade, and that was the reason why I came to Belgrade. After several days, I was received by Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you talk about with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he was very angry. He criticised the opposition as traitor, especially Vuk Draskovic, describing him as a traitor, that they were working against the Serbian national interests and that Draskovic was in cohorts [as interpreted] with Tudjman and Mesic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you explain why you were called to Belgrade to participate in a counter-rally? Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I represented the Serbs of Krajina, and Milosevic wanted the public to know that the Serbs of Krajina supported him, so that he could restore support for him in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you returned to Knin at that time, did you get a call from Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of March, between 11.00 and 12.00, at midday, by telephone. And he said, "Support Yugoslavia," and I said, "Fine," and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say in which way you should support Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing specific, but I understood he meant that we should declare our support for remaining in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you understand it this way? Did you discuss that beforehand with him, or where does your understanding come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the -- of his position. That was his position. That was my understanding of what he advocated, what he stood for, what kind of political idea he upheld.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually then act accordingly in the Krajina to this wish to support Yugoslavia? What did you do? Not you personally, but the Krajina authorities do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Executive Council of SAO Krajina decided to secede from Croatia, and this proposal was sent for adoption to the Municipal Assembly, and the assemblies and communes undertook to adopt this. So Krajina seceded from Croatia and in that way remained within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have three documents related to this issue, and it's -- they are all three in the -- in Exhibit 351. It's tab 22, tab 64, and tab 65, and they should briefly be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the first document is a decision of the -- of 18 March 1991 of the Assembly of the Knin Municipality, as part of the SAO Krajina, amending the statute of the SAO Krajina to expunge references to Croatia, in favour of "Federation." The second document is a decision dated 18 March 1991, same date, of the Assembly of Knin to secede from Republic of Croatia. And the third document is actually a similar -- is related to the municipalities of Drnis, Sinj, and Sibenik, and it's also on the 18th March 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving the interpretation. Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need to discuss this document further. Witness, we are still in March 1991. Are you aware that Milosevic and Tudjman met in March 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic told me, and later on I heard it from others as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Milosevic tell you, and when did you meet him in this effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of March 1991, that's when it happened, and he brought in a map on that occasion, a map of the former Yugoslavia, with the republican borders on it. He placed it on the table. He took his thumbnail and drew a line, as if he was separating a portion, breaking away the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, near Bihac, and with this gesture and incision, he said, "Tudjman needs Bihac." And then he added, "He needs a road between Benkovac and Drnis too." And I remained rigid. I didn't react at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you rigid? What did it mean for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was stunned because it meant everything -- it meant quite the opposite to what he had been saying up until then, that the SAO Krajina had the right to remain in Yugoslavia and that the JNA would protect it. And in this way, it was -- having said this, it was quite obvious that it would be Croatian territory, together with Bihac. Bihac is between SAO Krajina and the other parts of Yugoslavia, towards Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness the Exhibit 326, tab 11. That's actually the map that you yourself provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you show us which sections Mr. Milosevic actually cut out with his thumbnail, as you said? Can you show this on the map to us with the pointer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made an incision with his thumbnail along this direction. Bihac is up there. So this is the Bihac region and Cazinska Krajina. And this is what he did, a very sharp movement downwards, and then he pointed to the area above with his finger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you show it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He needed a road between Benkovac and Drnis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Witness, did Mr. Milosevic react in any way to your rigid reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go into open session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we have already heard from other witnesses of the Plitvice events, and we would not need to go into much detail. But can you tell us what was planned in -- whether there was a police station, a Serb police station, planned in the Plitvice region at that time? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who made this decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was made by the authorities in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you make this decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian government had announced that in the Plitvice area it would set up a separate municipality, so that Plitvice would be set aside from the Korenica municipality. And it was an area of the Plitvice Lakes National Park, which was very important to the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was actually -- who was given the task to establish the police station, and was it really established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretary of the SUP of SAO Krajina, Milan Martic, did not set up the police station, but armed persons were deployed there, members of the police force and others, in different ways, but not through the establishment of a police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that again the so-called parallel structure that you mentioned? Was it active there then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this structure then clash with the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an armed conflict, and people were killed in it. After that, the Croatian police force took control of Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the JNA intervene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA did intervene, yes, several hours after the Croatian police forces had taken control of Plitvice, and they deployed between the Plitvice area and the municipality and the village of Korenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the JNA then stay in control of the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It held the zone there, that area, up until August. At the end of August, it expelled the Croatian police and took control of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "August," August which year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was MUP Serbia personnel involved in this event in Plitvice? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They knew about these preparations. Now, how far they themselves took part in it and organised it, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they knew about these preparations, what do you mean "they"? Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people from the DB, the State Security Service of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which person precisely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, I don't know who was actually there, but a man from the group that was there permanently or, rather, at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, with the help of the usher, I would like to put to you two documents that reflect also what happened at that time, and it's Exhibit 352, tab 36 and 35. It is the decision -- the decision of the Executive Council of the SAO Krajina, dated the 1st of April, 1991, on the joining of the SAO Krajina to the Republic of Serbia, and actually the Official Gazette publishing this decision; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who drafted the declaration, and whose idea was it? And if needed, then we can go into private session. I'm not sure now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The draft was made by Borivoj Rasuo, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it also his initiative to do that, and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was his initiative, yes, to provoke Serbia, to intervene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To intervene in what? In which way, and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To become involved in the protection of the region and to see that it remained in Yugoslavia, outside Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it provoke a reaction from Belgrade? Did Mr. Milosevic, in particular, react?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was very sharp reaction on Mr. Milosevic's part, and he telephoned through the military base in Bihac, and he called me up in my flat and asked me to deny all this and to have the decision rescinded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give you -- did he give you a reason why he was opposing it? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that we have to come out in favour of Yugoslavia, declare ourselves in favour of Yugoslavia and not in favour of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you why, why it was so important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time and later on -- no, he didn't say clearly why. He just said Yugoslavia. He kept saying Yugoslavia. But the reason was quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that his direct links and links with Serbia would not be seen, links to what was happening in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you come to this conclusion? What is the basis of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the many conversations and from much of what he said and from his concept of how to realise his political goal, and that concept was quite simply to make it appear that other people were stepping down from Yugoslavia, whereas that part of Yugoslavia which he envisaged to remain in a newly organised state should appear to have remained there in a passive way and not by taking action. And he said the Serbs have the right to remain in Yugoslavia. The JNA will protect those areas. Peoples have a right to self-determination. Let the Croats leave. Let them go.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go into open session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did -- actually, did the authorities in the Krajina reverse their decision then and change it into remaining in Yugoslavia after this intervention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After later interventions, they did do so, yes. After the interventions were repeated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Repeated by whom? Who intervened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to put to you now another document, and it's also related to the 1st of April, 1991, and it's Exhibit 352, tab 38. Witness, it is a request or, rather, it's an order, a mobilisation order, and this mobilisation order of the 1st of April, 1991, there is a conclusion in this order saying the following: "We request from the Government of the Republic of Serbia that the forces of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia provide technical and personnel support to the SUP of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina." Is that related to what you called to provoke Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a call to realise the promises of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the situation so severe at that time in Plitvice that you -- that you in the Krajina felt it necessary to mobilise and to do these actions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was highly dramatic, to such an extent that it appeared that the Croatian government would take control of the entire region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned that MUP Serbia staff was already on the ground. You mentioned in Plitvice there was a person, and you mentioned that staff came, additional staff came. Who did come to the SAO Krajina in April 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say before I answer that there was one man I saw in Knin and not at Plitvice, before the events of Plitvice took place. And he came to Knin. That is to say Jovica Stanisic came to Knin. Franko Simatovic came, Fica, Captain Dragan, and several others. I don't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you meet Frenki Simatovic for the first time and what were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of April 1991. Jovica Stanisic brought him to my flat and introduced him to me as somebody who was an expert in different areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was -- was there a subordinate relationship between the two of them? Was one of them the superior of the other or were they equal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that Stanisic was the senior of the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they want from you? Why did they meet you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To see where I lived. And I had moved to a new apartment at the time. They said that they wanted to check and see whether my flat was being tapped by the army, among other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why by the army? And which army; the Croatian army or the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They meant the JNA. At least, that's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why would they suspect the army to do things like this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume because the army had services of this kind and monitored what citizens were doing, especially public persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you meet Captain Dragan for the first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April 1991 in the Golubic youth centre, which later became a camp of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go into open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did it become a camp, and what kind of a camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a training camp, a camp used for training of the DB, the state security, and the Krajina police force. And they trained the armed formations there and armed units were formed as a result. They were organised as a Special Police Unit and the volunteer detachments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those people trained there. First of all, how many people were trained there at a time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The training took place in a short space of time, perhaps ten days. At least, that's what I was told. And the groups numbered up to a hundred persons, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which time period did this camp function; from when to when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April 1991 until August 1991. In August, there was another training centre at Vukovic near Benkovac, as far as I know, and I heard that something similar existed at Samarica, but I didn't see that third Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. one myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge in this training camp in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franko Simatovic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he tell you that, that he was in charge there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first half of May, 1991. I was called to -- I was invited to go to the centre, and he was the host there, and he showed me around. He showed me what they were doing in the centre, in and around the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have a shooting range?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They had a shooting range between Golubic and Strmica, on the right side of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Simatovic show you this shooting range, and did he explain something about the equipment there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. When he showed me round the centre in the youth settlement of Golubic, he took me to the shooting range. And I didn't see the actual targets that were usually shot at, but there was a gun or a machine-gun of some sort, an anti-aircraft gun, multiple-barrelled. And he showed me this device and said that they had used it to shoot at the Croatian policemen in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you visited this Golubic camp, what was the state in -- in May 1991? What was the state of organisation? Did they have files on people they trained? How -- what was the grade of, degree of organisation there? Was it run professionally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Nikola Manovic, who was the assistant to secretary Martic, showed me the records and files for each municipality and for all the recruits at the centre, the trainees. I asked him whether there were any people from Knin, and he said, "Yes, of course," and he opened a separate drawer and showed me all the files. I took a brief look, but I didn't recognise the names, and I didn't go into that any more. And there were people there in uniforms, with long-barrelled weapons. They were well-disciplined, their hair was neatly cut, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go into open session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, does that mean that people from all municipalities were trained there, all municipalities from the SAO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people also equipped there with weapons and uniform and other equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uniforms and long-barrelled weapons, yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those people trained there, did they later become members of the police or the TO, or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They became members of the special police force, or "milicija," and members of the so-called volunteer detachments, whose name was changed later on, and they became known as units of the Territorial Defence later on, but in structure they remained the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Simatovic was in charge of the camp. What role did Captain Dragan have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a training instructor to begin with, and later on he commanded one of the units of the special police forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the only trainer or were there also other trainers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was his deputy, if he had any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had several deputies, or "komandirs," in his units. I don't know that he actually had a deputy, but he had subordinates, commanding officers, in his unit under him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a certain Ciga Simic, a trainer there and sort of commander of a unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was a commander. I don't know whether he was an instructor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the relationship between Frenki Simatovic and Captain Dragan? Was Captain Dragan a subordinate of Frenki?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a subordinate, but as far as I know, their relations are comradely. In terms of hierarchy, however, he was subordinate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Milan Martic, how was he -- what was his subordination situation, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was actually subordinate, or under the influence of people from the State Security Service of Serbia, and Slobodan Milosevic personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know -- to whom was -- you said he was actually subordinated or under the influence. To whom was he subordinated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ultimately, it was Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the way Milosevic treated him. I had personal insight into this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you have opportunity to see Mr. Milosevic treat Mr. Martic? How often did you see them together, and how did he treat him then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I saw them together was in August, between the 9th and 10th of August, and the 15th or 16th of August, 1991, in President Milosevic's office in Belgrade. On other occasions later, I saw them in 1995, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you saw them, how did he treat Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a person who was expected to obey him, as someone who was his man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did, for instance, Mr. Milosevic give him instructions or even orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in August he asked to become the commander of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina. Later on, I know -- I heard from Martic that he instructed him not to accept the Z-4 plan for the resolution of the political status of the Krajina which had been offered by the international community. I know, because Milosevic personally told me, that he gave him orders concerning military activities in the area of Livanjsko Polje on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Mr. Milosevic tell you that? What was the occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About Livanjsko Polje, in early April 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did it come that Mr. Milosevic talked to you about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked a meeting with Milosevic, as Minister of Foreign Affairs in the government of the Republic of Krajina. I wanted his opinion about the Z-4 plan and I wanted to complain to him that the Croatian army, the HVO from Bosnia and Herzegovina, was threatening Knin across the Dinara mountain chain. And I took with me a sketch, a map, to show him what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And how, then, did these talks end up with Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milosevic said -- this was a conversation with Milosevic in April, and it was about Martic and General Mladic. Milosevic took the map I had brought. He showed the territory, the wedge that had been made by the Croatian forces on Livanjsko Polje, and he said, "I have already told Mladic and Martic to cut this off." And then he indicated a direction from Glamoc to Dinara. He showed the line where he had told them to cut it off.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the map again, tab 11, tab 11 of the Exhibit 326.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it on this map, or ...? Witness, is this part on the map, or would you need another one to show us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be found on this map, but it's not very visible. It can't really be seen well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can use, actually, this municipality map, and it is -- I have here a smaller version that fits on the ELMO, and it is actually Exhibit 333. It's a small version. You should have that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us what Mr. Milosevic showed you on the map? Can you tell us which municipalities there are? Because we can only see the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the municipality of Livno and Bosanski Grahovo on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Croatian forces, starting in November and December 1994, had broken through Livanjsko Polje, in the direction of Grahovo, and taken a wedge-shaped area here, and Milosevic indicated that he had told Mladic and Martic to cut it off in this direction here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Mladic and Martic at that time cooperating there and involved in military actions together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military operations were being conducted there by the army and militia of Republika Srpska. I don't know to what extent the forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina took part in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We can go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back into open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned a certain Fica as well. Was he also a person from the Serbian MUP, or who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from him personally that he was from the personal bodyguard of President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did he have in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one of the instructors from the State Security Services of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Golubic camp, or where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Golubic, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that later on other camps, similar camps, were organised. Who was in charge in the camp in the Benkovac area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Captain Dragan, that he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also such a place in Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was in Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that it was Frenki's private base, not a military base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was there that made it Frenki's private base? Who was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frenki had an assistant who had some connections with Kistanje. His name was Goran Starcevic. I think this was one of the places where he stayed around Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a police formation there, or what do you consider a base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His place of residence, his and that of his assistants. It wasn't a military or a police base. It was where he lived. That's how I understood this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the conflict in Croatia, that is, summer 1990 to winter 1991, was Frenki actually constantly in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frenki was in the SAO Krajina, as far as I know, on two -- two times. The first time was from around the 8th of August, 1991, and then from September and throughout 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me clarify something. You said earlier on that you actually saw Frenki in April 1991. Now you say from around the 8th of August, 1991, you saw him. Is there a mistake in the year? Let us just clarify. When did he come to the -- when did he come to stay in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April 1991. That's when he came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned the 8th of August. What date does that mean, or is that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1991. 1991. That was when he was supposed to leave the Krajina. I assumed that he had left as of that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did he return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in September 1991. He was there again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the same apply to Captain Dragan, the same periods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Captain Dragan left in early August, on the 7th or 8th of August, 1991, and came back again sometime in November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, if that's a convenient moment, we will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we have mentioned now several armed formations outside of the army, the JNA, police, special police, TO, MUP, Serbian MUP. Was there a clearly defined command structure linking all these groups? Was there a clearly -- clearly a command structure, how these all fit together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the command structure from the top down to the municipality level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two lines of command or chains of command. One line went through the Presidency of Yugoslavia, the JNA, and the Territorial Defence units directly under its command. The other line went through the State Security Service of Serbia, that is the Ministry of Interior of Serbia, and through a parallel structure, the milicija or police of the Krajina and special volunteer units and the regular police and the groups belonging to the state security service. At the top of both lines was Slobodan Milosevic, or they coordinated and subordinated themselves on the ground while engaging in operations, however, these two lines were quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Joint actions, were there any joint actions between these two command structures, that is the military JNA structure and the police and volunteer structure? Did they conduct joint actions, and if so, who was then in command in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, they engaged in joint operations. I know from August 1991 onwards, it was the JNA that played a command role in these operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that already the police structure and on top of it you mentioned Mr. Milosevic, and you explained why you got to this, why you thought so and what your facts are to this effect. What -- why is Mr. Milosevic, as the President of Serbia, why is he on top of the JNA military structure? Did you get information to this effect, that he had this position in relation to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the main political figure, the most influential person, the most powerful person who had the political initiative, and he subordinated all other structures to his political initiative, that of Yugoslavia, including the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. I just wanted to ask the witness. Are you familiar with the concept of a Commander-in-Chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying that Mr. Milosevic was Commander-in-Chief of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Formally this was the Presidency of the SFRY, but de facto it was Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When -- how did Mr. Milosevic actually control or command the JNA, then, when he's not the formal commander? What -- how did he command the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- he ran part of the Presidency of the SFRY, the so-called Rump Presidency of the SFRY. He controlled them from the summer of 1991 onwards. He had influence over General Kadijevic, the federal Secretary for National Defence, and General Adzic who was the Chief of Staff of the JNA, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the basis of your knowledge? How do you know that? Did you actually see them together, the generals and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know they were together. Milosevic told me, and so did members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, I would like to ask one question. Mr. Witness, you said that Mr. Milosevic controlled the Presidency of the SFRY and some generals. If you are going to say some person is controlling over some persons, it should be different from that. They are -- from the fact that they are of the same opinion. Am I right? The Presidency of the Federal Republic are of the same opinion as the -- as Mr. Milosevic. How is it different? And if Milosevic is to control them, what are the whips and carrots? What are the consequences if they don't follow? Can you assist us with these questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I know, some members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, especially Jugoslav Kostic, told me that Milosevic was his chief. From the behaviour of Borisav Jovic, the president of the Presidency and later its member, he had the same attitude to Milosevic. He saw Milosevic as his superior, as someone in authority. Branko Kostic and Sejdo Bajramovic behaved in the same way. Milosevic himself said in July -- I think I've already spoken about this; he said to me and Karadzic, "Where should I deploy the army?" He behaved like a man who was able to deploy the army, to control it. I heard these words from him. In July, 1991, on another occasion, Milosevic invited me to his office, and when I arrived, his secretary said that the president was busy right then, that the generals were there. And then Milosevic came out and said he was meeting the generals. I can't remember now whether it was Adzic or Kadijevic I saw, whether he told me they were there, but that was the impression I gained, that the two of them were with him on that occasion. On the 26th of August, 1991, on another visit to Milosevic, when I visited him, he asked me about Spiro Nikolic, a general and commander of the Knin Corps. These are things that spring to mind right now, but I found out so many things. It wasn't just that they were of the same opinion, as His Honour said, but within that group, Milosevic was the leading authority. He was a sort of chief. He also had party mechanisms to influence people, like, say, Dobajramovic, Jugoslav Kostic, and Borislav Jovic. He could appoint them or replace them from their posts. And I also know from the events in October 1991 that he exerted influence in Montenegro through Branko Kostic. He influenced the leadership of Montenegro, Bulatovic and Djukanovic, and I don't know whether I can remember any other specific events at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There's no need to go into private session now. It's actually ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, returning back to Frenki Simatovic and to the SAO Krajina, I would like to put to you an exhibit, and it is tab 67 in Exhibit 352, and it's a report from the 5th or 6th August 1991 of the Serbian Autonomous District Krajina, 6th August 1991, report submitted by -- can you tell us who submits the report and to whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly who submitted it. One of the men belonging to this structure, the staff of the Territorial Defence, which was in the process of formation. It was submitted to the Prime Minister of Krajina, the secretary of the police of Krajina, the state security of Krajina, the command of the Territorial Defence, and to Frenki. The reference is to Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at the letterhead and the stamp, are they of the kind used at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the stamp that was used for this purpose, until the 30th of September, 1991, and the letterhead as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The supreme commander of the SAO Krajina TO that is here the first in the line of addressees, this is you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Prime Minister, according to the law that was implemented on the 1st of August, 1991, that should have been me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive this report and any other kinds of reports -- that kind of reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up to perhaps the 9th of August. Later there was some disruption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Frenki Simatovic also received such reports? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were sent to him. Now, whether he received them ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that the police and the parallel structure was financed through Serbia. You have explained that already. How about the costs for the training camps that we just mentioned? Who paid for the cost of the training camps and the arms, the weapons that were then distributed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all came from the MUP of Serbia, that is, from Serbia, through the state security service. Some uniforms were made by a local factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have mentioned, in regard of the weapons, that this came through a man called Braco Mihalj Kertes. How often did you meet this person, and how familiar are you with him and his voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times, five or six times perhaps. Five or six times. He has a specific tone of voice and his accent is rather like Vojvodina. It's not a typical Batva [phoen] accent, but it's rather like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet him in his office, and if so, where was it situated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did meet him, on the 4th of January, 1992. The office was above the office of President Milosevic. And I would also meet him in President Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Milosevic's offices, in the secretary's office one floor down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position did Mr. Kertes have and what was he doing in President Milosevic's office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the formal position that he held at the time. Earlier on, he was a member of the Presidency of Serbia. In 1991 and 1992, I don't know what actual position he held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met him, what did you talk with him about? What subject did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his office, the topic was -- somebody called me from the Presidency building - I think it was Jovica Stanisic - to tell me to come to the building, or one of them called me, on the 4th or 5th of January, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992. And when I arrived at the Presidency building, that is, the Presidency of Serbia, they told me at the entrance that I should go to Kertes's office, above Milosevic's offices. And I found Jovica Stanisic there; the chief of the counter-intelligence service of the State Security Service of Serbia, a man whose name I've forgotten, a large, heavily built man that looks like Frenki, but it's not Frenki. And Kertes accused me, in the presence of the other two, why we were opposed to the Vance plan and why we were disgracing President Milosevic, that we musn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to try it again with an intercept, and it is -- and I would rather ask you not to use this extra-small bundle of documents, because I think it's more confusing matters than adding -- helping and assisting you. I would therefore suggest you -- we can go into open session. I forgot to say that. I suggest you could simply use the intercept binder. It's actually tab 29 of 353. And for the technical booth, it's track 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we are actually playing the full intercept, and you can easily follow the English script, and the witness should have the B/C/S version. And maybe you can put it on the ELMO. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: RADOVAN KARADZIC: Hello? UNIDENTIFIED WOMAN: Good day. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Is Braco there? Radovan Karadzic speaking. UNIDENTIFIED WOMAN: Yes. One moment. RADOVAN KARADZIC: How are you? All right? UNIDENTIFIED WOMAN: Good. I saw you. You had your hair cut a bit. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. Ha ha. Well, they were preparing items ... have they shown ... UNIDENTIFIED WOMAN: Yes. The whole of it. RADOVAN KARADZIC: How much of this did they show? UNIDENTIFIED WOMAN: I watched it also on Yutel, and they showed a lot of it. That was the first time you emerged, as I would say, 'you've emerged from the holster.' RADOVAN KARADZIC: Uh-huh. UNIDENTIFIED WOMAN: Ha ha. Here you are. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Thank you. Hello. BRACO: And the same to you a thousand times over. RADOVAN KARADZIC: How are you? BRACO: Well, I'm busy. RADOVAN KARADZIC: I see. Tell me, do you have a lot of work to do? BRACO: I have, a lot. RADOVAN KARADZIC: A lot of work, haven't you? BRACO: This morning, I can say after Samarang it's much better. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Is it? BRACO: I didn't have time down there, because those from Montenegro had been there, the first and second ones. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Uh-huh. BRACO: I left. I didn't have time, but ... RADOVAN KARADZIC: I can see it's been busy ... BRACO: But I discussed matters with these ... RADOVAN KARADZIC: Uh-huh. BRACO: With those with 'stars.' RADOVAN KARADZIC: Oh, did you? BRACO: Yes. I sent them to fucking hell. RADOVAN KARADZIC: What do you mean? Go to fucking hell? BRACO: Well, I told them everything. RADOVAN KARADZIC: I see, I see. BRACO: I told them everything, that there would be convoys and convoys now. RADOVAN KARADZIC: I badly needed that, that ... BRACO: Yes. Yes. I passed all of that to them. Now, I've rung a friend, a countryman from the federal -- RADOVAN KARADZIC: This is where I need it, in this metropolis. Because if you don't take business premises in the metropole, and you don't open a shop in a metropolis ... BRACO: Yes. There must be flour, there should also be salt, there also must ... RADOVAN KARADZIC: There should be high-quality goods, this and that. BRACO: It should be well supplied, like a supermarket. RADOVAN KARADZIC: If you lose a metropolis in terms of trade, if you don't corner it ... BRACO: Of course. Of course. RADOVAN KARADZIC: That is where the main battle is fought, and if you don't succeed there ... BRACO: Well, of course. And you know what? The most important thing is that the locations are attractive. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes, that's true. A pedestrian zone, where people ... BRACO: Well, of course. And when it's painted, it should be clear what is yellow, what is white, and slowly -- RADOVAN KARADZIC: Exactly! Excellent! That's good. Apart from that? So you're in a better mood today, aren't you? BRACO: I am. However, on Saturday I wanted to kill myself. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Oh, my. Was it then? BRACO: Well, I have been having a hard time, guys. You have no idea how hard. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes, yes. BRACO: I know. I mean, I've been having a truly hard time. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. Yes. BRACO: I can see the needs, I can see everything. There's grain, flour, everything in Vojvodina ... RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. BRACO: It's been left there lying around in stock. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. Yes. And nothing -- BRACO: Well, it's expensive since it's in bloody stock. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. Yes. Of course. Yeah, the storage itself is expensive! BRACO: Yes. RADOVAN KARADZIC: They've risen the costs of storage just like that. BRACO: Yes. RADOVAN KARADZIC: And mice ... BRACO: Have you spoken to the manager? RADOVAN KARADZIC: No, I haven't. BRACO: Of commodity reserves? You haven't? RADOVAN KARADZIC: No, I haven't. He was busy, er ... BRACO: Er, you just carry on insisting and insisting ... Understand? RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. Yes. And on restocking the commodity reserves, so ... BRACO: Yes. RADOVAN KARADZIC: They should give us everything that is near its best-before date straight away. BRACO: Right. RADOVAN KARADZIC: And they should ... this for themselves, uh-huh ... BRACO: That's right. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Fresh food to their storehouse. BRACO: Yes, that's right. RADOVAN KARADZIC: I think that our reputation will rise amongst people with this. BRACO: Well, you know, when people are not hungry and thirsty, then it's ... RADOVAN KARADZIC: Less difficult. BRACO: Uh-huh. Political situation is less difficult. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. And they can see that the party is doing something. BRACO: That's right. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Concerning those everyday matters. That's ... BRACO: True ... RADOVAN KARADZIC: And ... BRACO: That should be, and newspapers, there should be ... RADOVAN KARADZIC: Right. BRACO: Everything. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. Tell me what the political situation is like. Do you know anything? BRACO: Well, let me tell you, it's weird. Weird quietness. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Well, yes. They really want to go ... BRACO: I believe so. I've had some information this morning that every house will get a battery, which is very interesting. That means they will try with the blackout. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Uh-huh, their house, is it? BRACO: Yes. Yes. RADOVAN KARADZIC: And nobody is going to attack them, for fuck's sake. BRACO: No. No. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Where? In Slovenia or Slavonija? BRACO: I'm talking about Croatia. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Oh, Croatia?! BRACO: Yes. RADOVAN KARADZIC: So theirs ..., to get, to distribute batteries. BRACO: The HDZ will give everyone a battery. RADOVAN KARADZIC: How come they have so many batteries? Bloody hell. BRACO: I haven't got a clue. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Well, who is going to attack them? Are they mad? BRACO: Well, no. I think that they, that everyone, that is left in a cinema -- and they are attacking, and it's easier with batteries than without them! RADOVAN KARADZIC: Oh, I see. Yes. So they would attack ... anyway? BRACO: They have, they have a safe plan. Everything has been worked out. You see, when you do that and see what you've done, then you will need a battery. RADOVAN KARADZIC: And when, when would, er, you expect that? BRACO: On Vidovdan, the latest. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Fucking bastards. BRACO: I think Vidovdan, because Serbs will relax then. RADOVAN KARADZIC: I see. I see. BRACO: And so on. I've been trumpeting that everywhere and ... RADOVAN KARADZIC: It should be given to newspapers. It should be given to newspapers. BRACO: And I've been sending all kinds of messages. Serbs on Vidovdan, in a dignified manner, but do not detach yourselves from everything. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Right. Right. BRACO: From the families and so on. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Fuck. That's disheartening, but this with food is heartening now. BRACO: Are you, are you at work, in your office? RADOVAN KARADZIC: I'm at work, but I will take two or three days' leave. BRACO: You'll take a leave? RADOVAN KARADZIC: I'll take few days' leave, because I have political -- I have to calm down a bit. Krajina, er, wants to secede and join the other Krajina. BRACO: Oh, God, oh, God. That's ... RADOVAN KARADZIC: I have to calm the fools down, and ... BRACO: Well, that's ... RADOVAN KARADZIC: They make some decisions, but they can't carry this one out now and in that way. BRACO: Oh, fucking bastards, are they crazy? RADOVAN KARADZIC: That's only in case somebody is seceding from Yugoslavia and ... BRACO: Well, it's clear. And the moment they secede, it's clear. RADOVAN KARADZIC: It is clear. BRACO: And then we mustn't wait. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Right. No. BRACO: Then we mustn't. RADOVAN KARADZIC: We, we'll then secede from Yugoslavia and that's it. BRACO: That's how it was ... rump Yugoslavia. RADOVAN KARADZIC: No matter how big it is. It would be better if it were big, but ... BRACO: Well, we are fighting for a big one, for the current one, whatever the outcome. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. There will be a small one at least and ... BRACO: That's right. RADOVAN KARADZIC: So it has started well, hasn't it? BRACO: Yes. RADOVAN KARADZIC: I see. You haven't seen the manager of the commodity reserves, so you will, er ... BRACO: Yes. Yes. Don't worry. I'll go to the manager of the commodity reserves. Just to see, you know? RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. Yes. BRACO: So that he hurries the responsible officers about the request. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Understand the gravity. Because if starvation sets in, you won't be able to do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Stop. I have one question to the translation booth. I think there is a word, and a quite significant word, missing. Can we replay that short sequence where Mr. Radovan Karadzic says: "I see. You haven't seen the manager of the commodity reserves..."? And I think you missed a word there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But we can stop with intercept playing here at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear -- did you listen to this intercept before during -- during your conversations here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- do you know the voices of the people speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised the voice of Radovan Karadzic and Braco Kertes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff. I need some kind of clarification from the interpreter. I understand that they said the interpreters are reading from the script, not interpreting from the voice or the Serbian version. They just read it.

utterances.text: Yes, they just read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I understood they would check it with the voices or the B/C/S version. You don't do that?
