utterances.text: The sound is so bad it's simply impossible. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to have these tapes properly checked at some stage by some independent body such as our own translation services.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, you will have these intercepts. Actually, they are part of the exhibit. And when you listen in to them personally, you will see that the quality is much better when you play it on a normal machine with that same CD. The witness has already mentioned it several times. But the witness, I think, would be able to clarify that matter that I wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. But the point that I'm making is that we will need this checked by our own translation services in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will take care of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Witness, let me ask you a question in relation to the contents of the tape. These two persons that you recognised speaking, they speak about food. They speak about supermarket. They speak about batteries. Is that what was really traded and shifted at that time from Vojvodina to other places within Yugoslavia? Do you know that? Do you have any information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This, for me, is an intercept, though there was flour and sugar so it was -- but that is not what they were referring of. They -- they were speaking figuratively. I would say it would be a mildly coded conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are they talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're talking about weapons, what Kertes was -- that was his field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've come to the same problem we've come to throughout in dealing with these intercepts, of interpretation by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If a foundation can be laid for his opinion, then he can give it for what it's worth. If he has a similar experience or something of that sort. If it's merely an opinion, then of course it's purely worthless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We haven't got there yet to say whether it is a proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you get the point. It's merely for this witness to say they're thinking about something else -- talking about something else. It's merely his opinion unless he's got something to base it on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness had actually already explained that he was shown weapons by a certain person, and we spoke about that in private session, and he said that this person mentioned that these weapons were received through Braco, and he also said that Braco --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think this is all a matter of argument. You can certainly --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can certainly put that to us. We will have to consider it. But I don't think we can hear the witness's opinion on this any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Karadzic says in relation to the manager of the commodity reserves -- do you recall that you discussed this and you heard this before in the Prosecution's office when you heard, did you find a mistake in the translation when we discussed it? What does Mr. -- when you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we have a look at the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can such a question be put as to whether he found an error in the translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can say if he found it. We'll have it checked. He can say what his opinion is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. He can say, "I listened to this and this is what I heard." What it's worth, of course, is a totally different matter. Yes. Briefly, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Karadzic makes a remark in relation to the manager of the commodity reserves, and in the B/C/S version: RADOVAN KARADZIC: I see. You haven't seen the manager of the commodity reserves... Can you find this, please? And can we put it on the -- do you have this? And Braco actually then says: BRACO: Yes. Yes. Don't worry. I'll go to the manager of the commodity reserves. Just to see, you know? It's rather at the end of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. It said that it wasn't the chief of the commodity reserves but Slobodan Milosevic, if that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 3 of the Serbian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. version, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the telephone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't correct him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honours, there are actually twice mentioning of the manager. It's first on page 3, but then also at the end of the conversation. It should be on the second to last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got a copy to give to the witness with it highlighted?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He's actually -- yes. And can you give the witness ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have this section where Mr. Radovan Karadzic says: RADOVAN KARADZIC: I see. You haven't seen the manager of the commodity reserves... Can you please read this? It is marked. It's marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just put it in front of the witness. Let us not waste any more time. Put the marked passage in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you please read the two sentences in your language, and can we have the translation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: RADOVAN KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Fine. Down there to the chief of the commodities, you haven't been there. So you will. BRACO: Yes. Yes. Don't worry. I'm going to see the chief of the commodity reserves to see only, you understand? RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you can see, the word "down there" is missing in the English version that we have, and it was just translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As I say, we'll have this matter properly translated. Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can put this away now. I would like to put two documents to you in relation to this matter. The first one is Exhibit 352, tab 40, and it's a request by Milan Martic to Jovica Stanisic and Milan Tepavcevic at the state security department of the MUP to determine expenditure. And just to look at the stamp and the signature. Is that -- and the header. Is that what was used, and is it Mr. Martic's signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the letterhead and the stamp, but the signature is not Martic's, though his name is indicated. It says "For Martic," so somebody signed on his behalf. It says, "For the Minister, Milan Martic." So somebody else signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other document is tab 41 in that same exhibit, and it's a letter by Nebojsa Pavkovic to Radomir Stojicic of the 22nd of March, 1995, in relation to training centres. And again I would like just to -- you to speak about the letterhead, the stamp, and the signature. Is that what was used at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Pavkovic was the deputy, but I can't recognise the signature. I don't remember what his signature was like. But everything else fits, so probably that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this letter is addressed to the Ministry of Interior, MUP, Mr. Radovan Stojicic, and it's about the help in relation to Sabotage Squad training. Do you know, was such a cooperation between the MUP Serbia and the MUP of the SAO still ongoing at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. I heard about it. I don't know specifically which men were involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Witness, I would like to return with you now to meetings with Mr. Milosevic, and we have already touched on referenda that were conducted in 1991. Did the Assembly of the SAO also hold a referendum in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was put to the voters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the SAO Krajina to be joined to the Republic of Serbia and to remain with Serbia and Montenegro within Yugoslavia and others who want to remain in there. It was first decided that they should vote on being conjoined to Serbia, but then it was changed. The question was changed upon the intervention of Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by the "intervention of Mr. Milosevic"? What kind of an intervention was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked that we state our views and vote for Yugoslavia and not for Serbia. And he was angry because of the referendum. He was also angry because we had said we'd be sending a commission to inform the Assembly of Serbia about the results of the voting at the referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally speak with Mr. Milosevic on this occasion, and if so, where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. At the beginning of May, in his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he want you to do, and did you actually then react to his wishes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To come out in favour of Yugoslavia, to say yes to Yugoslavia. And he said that some academicians had told him that I should be killed because I was so stubborn, a troublemaker, and I was constantly upsetting matters. However, I left him saying the opposite, or, rather, saying what had already been established, determined. And later on - I can't remember now - some other people insisted that we supplement this question and that's what was, in fact, done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was, at the end, the question to put to the voters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Are you in favour of joining up with Serbia and remain in Yugoslavia with the others who wish to remain in Yugoslavia?" So the question asked of the voters was expanded. To join up with Serbia and remain in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go into open session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back into open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to put actually the documents dealing with the referendum to the witness just briefly. It's tab 30. It's all in the binder 351. It's tab 30, tab 32, tab 33, and tab 35, all dealing with the referendum, the decision to conduct it, the report on the referendum, the list of municipalities who voted, and a decision of the SAO Krajina electing a deputy group to present results of the referendum to the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia. Witness, we do not need to discuss this document. It's just for you to just see. That's all correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this delegation that was mentioned in the last document, was it actually received by the National Assembly of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was received by the vice-president of the Assembly, Borivoj Petrovic, in private, and took them out to dinner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the result of -- what was the result, and what happened after the referendum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the referendum, what happened was that the Assembly of the SAO Krajina proclaimed the results of the voting at the referendum, and after that, the SAO Krajina constituted itself again anew as a federal territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have discussed the police situation in the Krajina, and the military situation, and I would -- I would like to go into private session for the next sequence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- did the government of the SAO Krajina ever have any control over Martic and any police force within the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to change that in April -- in spring 1991, and if so, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did try at the end of May 1991, and instead of the Minister of the Interior, that Martic should be replaced and be the Minister of Defence and that both these men be responsible to the government of the SAO Krajina. And the Assembly did in fact elect Martic as Defence Minister, but he didn't want to hand over his militia -- hand over the militia, police force. And on the 27th of June, 1991, he forced the issue, and he was given that post again. That is to say he was re-elected to the post that he continued to hold, in fact, throughout that time. And according to what people from the police force told me, he did this with the help of Frenki and the people around Frenki.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back into open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to -- I would like to put to the witness now the document tab 54 -- 54, yes, in Exhibit 352. It's a decision on the formation of a Special Purpose Unit of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina to be called the Krajina Police, and to be under the authority of the Ministry of Defence. The task of the -- according to Article 2: "The task of the Krajina Police shall be to defend the territory ... of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina, secure vital facilities, the Region's institutions and other tasks within the domain of internal affairs." According to this task, is that actually a regular police task?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been the territorial police force, a sort of gendarmerie. That's what it should have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was the plan.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- it's in here in this decision. It's actually said that the Ministry of Defence should be in charge of this. And I have here as the next document the exhibit -- tab 55, Exhibit 352, and it's actually the decision to appoint Mr. Milan Martic in this position that you just mentioned. And the next exhibit is tab 55 of that same --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- 56 of that same document, and it is the election of -- a decision on the election of the Minister of Interior, and it's (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Martic agree to this while this decision was made on the 29th of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day he did agree and took the oath of office as Defence Minister, but the very next day he didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who told you that this was according to an influence of Frenki Simatovic? Who told you that, and how did you hear of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from the police force, the police station in Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to put to you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Martic told me, too, himself. He said, "I don't want to."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did (redacted), did he try to take over his function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did try, yes, to take over his function, and he appointed some people. The head of the police station in Knin, that was a new man, and a deputy for him. However, as far as I heard, people from the police force said that Martic and the others, that people tore up the documents and laughed, and he didn't try and do it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that I actually need to put the two witnesses -- exhibits to the witness. It's actually what he said already. It's the confirmation of appointing on the 27th of June, 1991, (redacted) to be the Minister of Urban Planning, Housing, and Public. And the Minister of Interior of the Serbian Autonomous Region is then appointed, Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the politicians in the Krajina try to get control over the police in August 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, through the organisation of Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic was appointed deputy commander of the Territorial Defence, and he applied the law according to which the police force should be subjected -- subjugated to the Territorial Defence, the command of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, that was actually not my question, and I think I will put to you a document, and that is the tab 62 from Exhibit 352, and it is a decision of the government of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina of the 1st of August, 1991, to abolish the state security service on the territory of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina. Can you tell us what the background of this decision was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The background was the following: To exempt the influence of the State Security Service of Serbia and the DB in Krajina, which was part of the State Security Service of Serbia, and to gain control and influence over the internal affairs department, the police force, in Krajina. That meant that the Ministry of the Interior should be under the control, placed under the control, of the government. That was an attempt that was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, was Mr. Stanisic in Knin, and did you discuss this step with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, Stanisic was in Knin, and I met him there. He asked me what happened, and I said that the government would set up an agency for national security of its own. He just sort of grinned. He was mocking me sarcastically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at the same time also try to establish control over the armed groups that were not part of the police? Did you try to establish a TO controlled by the SAO authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. The Territorial Defence was under the competency of the municipal staffs of Territorial Defence under the JNA. The JNA had the keys to its weapons, and I wanted to combine the Territorial Defence of SAO Krajina to set up a Main Staff, main headquarters, and that the Territorial Defence should come under the Prime Minister and government of SAO Krajina as the executive personage.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go into open session again, and I would like to put a decree to the witness. It's tab 63 of Exhibit 352.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this decision a decree on the insignia worn by member of the armed forces, Territorial Defence, and Special Purpose Units of the SAO Krajina? Is that related to the matter that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the TO actually succeed in becoming an independent institution controlled by the SAO government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened? Who resisted it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic helped set up a Main Staff of the Territorial Defence, but it was subordinate to the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you also have a clash with --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would have to go into private session, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you have a clash also with Frenki Simatovic and Captain Dragan, and if so, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. At the beginning of August - I think it was around about the 8th or 9th of August - after these legal provisions had been adopted on Territorial Defence and after this decree, this document that was passed, he sent a man by the name of Djoko Majstorovic to take the insignia of the Territorial Defence to a club that was set up at the Knin fortress where the wartime staff of the Territorial Defence of Knin was to be lodged, and at that time it was the seat of Captain Dragan, Milan Martic, Frenki, and the men around them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise if I'm wrong, but as I can't hear the witness at all and I'm looking at the transcript, what he's saying, I understand that it is tab 63 that we're -- tab 63 is a decree of Milan Babic about insignia worn by members of the armed forces of the Territorial Defence, what the flag looks like, and the crossed swords on it, and I didn't understand that that was the subject upon which the explanation was given. Is that my mistake or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's moved on, and he's describing a clash with Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it's actually -- this clash is actually related to this exhibit, because it's about the flag and the insignia and the establishment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is that exhibit, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it's related to that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Witness, go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Are we in closed session?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to that on the -- at the Knin fortress which is where Captain Dragan, Frenki were, to see what was going on, because Captain Dragan told the man carrying the insignia that while he was there, Babic wouldn't be setting them up. And I went to see what was happening. When I arrived, the people there from the municipal headquarters of the Territorial Defence were dispersing. They said that Captain Dragan had let them go. They were there providing security for the area otherwise. And I arrived up there. I went into the meeting hall, the conference hall. I was told that Captain Dragan was there. Captain Dragan was in a meeting. He was having a conference with his unit, the unit, the special unit he was in command of. I went into the meeting room and sat next to him, and somebody said later on, told me that when I went in and sat down, Frenki got up and left the room. Nobody addressed me. Captain Dragan held a speech, continued to deliver his speech to his men, to his people. He said that it was -- that the politicians were to blame for everything and that he was leaving, he was going to leave Knin, and that he was going to leave his men to Frenki and that everything would be resolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you threatened on that day by anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Captain Dragan's men followed me to the centre in Golubic or part of Golubic, which is where the civilian structures of the Knin municipality were supposed to be deployed in case of war, and I had gone there to tell the men not to disperse, but I was followed there by Captain Dragan's men. They blocked the whole area and shouted, "Where's the man that has to be killed? Where is he?" And then I escaped from that locality and went to the neighbouring village. And in the morning, I called up President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you call him? What did you want from him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell him that those men around Frenki are idiots. They're mad. They don't know what they're doing. I was very much afraid, and I wanted to ask him to withdraw them from Krajina, and he promised that he would do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frenki. I'm sorry. I asked Frenki, that Frenki be withdrawn, quite specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you tell him? You said you told him that they were mad and what they were doing. What exactly did you tell him what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I explained this over the phone to him on that occasion. I didn't go into all the details on that occasion. I just gave a general assessment of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you ask for the removal of Frenki and not of Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frenki was the boss up there. He was in charge of those men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said Mr. Milosevic promised to -- that he would do that, and did he do that? Did Frenki --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Frenki around up there any more. I assume he did. I wasn't quite sure, but Frenki, on the 26th of August, 1991, was removed, and Milosevic said that Frenki should go back to Krajina again. And I assume that in this interim he had actually left Krajina. I mean Frenki.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we finish that sequence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he later -- you said Mr. Milosevic then said that Frenki should go back to the Krajina again. When did he say that? What were the circumstances of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of August, 1991, in his cabinet, when somebody conveyed a message to me from him that I should come to see him to a meeting there. And when I arrived, that was it. That was when he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Frenki then return to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-061 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did return, yes. I met him and heard about him in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, that finishes this sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll adjourn. Before we do so, I should say, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, by my calculation you've got four and three-quarter hours left. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Are we in open session? Let's go back into open session so people can hear.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn. Before we do, I should say, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you have four and three-quarter hours left with this witness and should plan accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I raise this issue of time today or do you want me to start with this tomorrow? Because I want to make a request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You want to?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I want to make a request for more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long more are you asking for?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm asking for two more days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two more days. That's another eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll think about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, shall I explain myself? Because this witness is of a very special type of witness, and for the Croatia section of the case, he is the only one of this type. And if we hear his entire evidence that he has to give, we can definitely drop other -- other lower-level insiders who can give us little pieces of the evidence that this witness can give us as a whole, and we could simply -- I'm not in a position at the moment to say who exactly would we drop. I can only say that people will be dropped. And actually, the Prosecution team is at the moment checking and already filtering out who can be dropped of the next lower-level insider witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just give us some idea so we know what the position is as to how many witnesses you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I can give you this idea tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But it will definitely be five or six people, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll think about that. Meanwhile, let me deal with one other general matter concerning sittings or hearings this term and into next. The first matter is this: that it seems there may be some rearrangement of the dates of the Plenary. It was fixed for the 10th to the 12th. Now, I don't know whether there will be or not, but fairly definitely we'll be sitting on what was the first day, the 10th. I think it's the 10th. It was the first day. I'm told it's the -- there seems to be some doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's the 11th is the first day of the Plenary. Our last sitting day was Tuesday the 10th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it's the 11th. We will definitely be sitting the 11th. It may be that we will look to sit the other days too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very helpful to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And dropping another day as a result of the rearrangement. But that is yet to be confirmed. It may not take place, but definitely the 11th. I suggest that we use the 19th, which is an odd day -- 18th of December, rather, the Wednesday. If necessary, of course, we'll finish a witness, but it may be sensible to use that for the administrative and other legal arguments, Mr. Torkildsen's evidence, for instance, and the various submissions we've had about the conduct of the trial. Again, closer to the time, we can arrange that. Finally, advance notice of January's sittings: The first break in January sittings will be between the 22nd and the 24th of January. I think the 24th of January may be a court maintenance day. I can't remember that definitely, but anyway, we will be breaking in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we will let you have a calendar, let everybody have a calendar for the next term, as it were, as soon as we can. Very well. Tomorrow morning, please.
